extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of communication studies and legal scholars interested in patent law and rhetorical analysis
extracted.subtask_short: rhetorical analysis of Alice patent decision
extracted.subtask_description: A qualitative rhetorical critique of the Supreme Court opinion in Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank that applies Perelman and Olbrechts‑Tyteca’s new rhetoric to understand how the Court framed patent-eligibility and the contours of an 'abstract idea.'

rubrics_metrics.name: New rhetoric — Audience (universal vs. particular)
rubrics_metrics.description: Perelman outlined two types of audiences, the universal audience and the particular audience. A universal audience represents all rational beings and humanity; a particular audience is a specific group with shared values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a universal audience use deductive reasoning with logic and facts; for a particular audience tailor arguments to shared values or establish a connection between warrants and the audience’s beliefs. In legal contexts, knowing Justices’ prior opinions and beliefs helps craft persuasive legal arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: New rhetoric — Solidity of claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The first tenet of new rhetoric is the solidity of claims: claims must be judged as reasonable, rather than absolute, and grounded in a reality acceptable to the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Toulmin model: claim (thesis), grounds (support), warrant (reasoning linking claim and grounds). Employ syllogisms for explicit formal reasoning and enthymemes when relying on premises implied by the audience’s beliefs. Claims should be 'real and preferable premises' so an audience can decode and accept them.

rubrics_metrics.name: New rhetoric — Liaison (association and dissociation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Liaison engenders techniques of association and dissociation among premises. Three techniques to create association are quasi-logical (abductive) reasoning, arguments based on the structure of reality, and arguments establishing a structure of reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use association to infer cause-and-effect (example: plaintiff inferring negligence from distracted driving). Use dissociation to separate letter and spirit of a rule to justify a particular outcome (example: driver violating a sidewalk rule to avoid harm). Effective liaison links facts and legal conclusions; ineffective liaison weakens persuasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: New rhetoric — Presence (kairos/timing and significance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence determines how to give significance to premises and relationships in an argument; it emphasizes the content and the relationship between rhetor and audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider timing (kairos) and social significance when framing legal arguments. In patent disputes, presence can be shown by the case’s journey (e.g., reaching the Supreme Court), indicating public/legal importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: New rhetoric — Ambiguity and its contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Language is ambiguous and ambiguity occurs in four contexts: (1) no previous applicable rule because the case is the first to discuss the issue; (2) a previous ruling is subject to more than one meaning; (3) when a previous ruling is claimed to be invalid; and (4) conflict exists between two potentially applicable rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and articulate ambiguity when analyzing legal texts; ambiguity is inherent to language and affects how claims are perceived and adjudicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent-eligible subject matter under 35 U.S.C. §101
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 101 defines patent-eligible subject matter as 'Whoever invents or discovers any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use §101 as the statutory baseline for eligibility analysis but account for judicially-created exceptions (laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract idea exclusion (judicially recognized exception under §101)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court held that laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas are implicitly exempted from being patented; abstract ideas cannot be patented because permitting a patent to an abstract idea 'would effectively grant a monopoly over an abstract idea.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether a claim is 'directed to' an abstract idea (e.g., intermediated settlement, risk hedging). If so, examine whether the claim adds something significantly more than the abstract idea itself; mere recitation of a generic computer implementing the idea is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent claims must do more than apply an abstract idea on a generic computer
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent that 'does nothing more than ... provide instruction to apply an abstract idea ... through a generic computer' is not patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the claim improves an existing technology or technological process (a meaningful technological contribution) versus merely automating a known abstract practice with generic computer components. Alice’s claims failed because they were 'too generic' and did not improve technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement/technical contribution requirement for eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: To be patent-eligible the patent should 'improve upon an existing technology or technological process' rather than merely describe a fundamental economic practice implemented on conventional technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for specific technical mechanisms or a demonstrated technological advance; lacking such association weakens eligibility under the Court’s reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty/innovation as relative standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Innovation is characterized by a novel creation or some remarkable advancement of an already existing artifact or concept; characterizing innovation is relative to existing things and contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate novelty relative to the prior art and the relevant technical field; recognize that determining novelty often requires specialized knowledge and context-sensitive judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity versus vagueness of patent claims (vagueness increases litigation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vague patents, especially those grounded on abstract concepts, increase the likelihood of litigation and can be exploited for rent-seeking behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims with clarity and precise scope to reduce downstream litigation risk; courts and commentators note that vague/abstract claims facilitate NPE litigation and judicial uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-practicing entity (NPE)/patent troll behavior as evaluative factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent trolls (NPEs) are plaintiffs who own patents without intending to commercialize them and instead seek royalties, often using litigation as a business strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the patent owner’s behavior and incentives (practicing vs non-practicing) when assessing social and policy consequences of patent enforcement; litigation cost asymmetries (high defense costs) affect outcomes and settlements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural criteria for Supreme Court certiorari and holdings
rubrics_metrics.description: A case must exhibit controversy, be heard in lower courts and appealed; the Supreme Court grants certiorari when four of nine Justices decide to hear a case. For the Court to render an official decision, at least five of nine Justices must agree on at least one legal argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that granting certiorari signals substantial controversy or a need to resolve circuit splits; a majority opinion is binding on lower courts while concurrences/dissents inform future argumentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of precedent and stare decisis in evaluating patent law
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges’ rulings occur within stare decisis; the Court references past opinions to determine how to treat abstract ideas and patent eligibility (e.g., Bilski v. Kappos).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze how prior cases frame categories like 'abstract idea' and how courts apply or distinguish precedent; inconsistencies or ambiguities in prior rulings create analytical challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonableness of opposing claims in litigation as a contextual evaluative factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims between parties in patent litigation must be 'reasonable' to be worth disputing in court; the presence of reasonable claims underlies judicial review and the Supreme Court’s willingness to accept a case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess both parties’ claims for factual basis and reasonableness; reasonable factual foundation contributes to procedural progress through the courts and demonstrates controversy.
